title: The Future of Migrant Caravans: Collective Resistance or the End of a Containment Strategy?
author: Carlos Calles
content:
_This article by Carlos Calles appears in the November 2026 issue of_ Let's
Talk About Migration _(_ Hablemos de Migración _), a magazine on migration
issues published by the Frente Amplio de Mexicanos y Migrantes.[Read and
download the full November
issue](https://diegotorres72.com/internacional/boletin-hablemos-de-
migracion-2/)._

![Let's Talk About Migration](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2025/06/image-1.png)

Since late 2018, Mesoamerican highways have been the stage for a phenomenon
that has drastically transformed the narrative of human mobility: migrant
caravans. These mass exoduses captured global attention, not only for their
scale but also for representing a bold survival strategy in the face of a
historically deadly journey. In the current landscape, marked by increasingly
stringent border policies and coercive diplomacy, an unavoidable question
arises: are caravans still a viable strategy for collective protection, or are
they definitively changing due to controls, deportations, and new
restrictions? To answer this question, it is essential to analyze how the
externalization of borders is beginning to dismantle a movement born from the
instinct for self-preservation.

Originally, the decision to travel in caravans arose as a response to terror
and utter vulnerability. Research by the Network for Documentation of Migrant
Advocacy Organizations (REDODEM) and the National Human Rights Commission
(CNDH) indicates that mass gatherings allowed thousands to confront a journey
besieged by kidnappings, extortion, and recruitment by organized crime.
Eduardo Torre Cantalapiedra, a researcher at El Colegio de la Frontera Norte
(El Colef), argues that these marches, from their inception, constituted a
vital source of protection and material support. This collective dynamic
facilitated the movement of vulnerable populations—such as single mothers with
children, unaccompanied minors, and members of the LGBTQ+ community supported
by specialized shelters like Casa Frida in Mexico City— with greater
guarantees of survival.

In addition to providing immediate physical security, these marches have
historically served as a vital "release valve" against administrative
collapse. Numerous journalistic reports and academic studies highlight that
transit cities located on Mexico's southern border, particularly Tapachula in
Chiapas, operate in practice as enormous "pressure cookers." Faced with the
dramatic backlog of immigration procedures at the Mexican Commission for
Refugee Assistance (COMAR) and the lack of local employment opportunities,
mass mobilizations have become the definitive means to break through the
state's containment barrier and demand respect for international asylum law.

Despite the legitimacy of the caravans as a tool for citizen self-defense, the
fierce government reaction has eroded their viability. Analytical reports
published by the Washington Office on Latin America (WOLA) and extensive
reports from the Migration Policy Institute (MPI) indicate that the United
States' constant coercive diplomacy has forced Mexico to undertake strict
punitive containment measures, effectively extending the U.S. southern border
to the Isthmus of Tehuantepec. Thus, the region's migration model has rapidly
shifted from humanitarian rhetoric to systematic policies of entrapment and
outright deterrence.

This metamorphosis becomes undeniably evident in the direct repression of the
migrants on the highways. According to alerts issued by the Migration Affairs
Program at the Ibero-American University, Mexican authorities such as the
National Migration Institute (INM) and the National Guard have deployed
violent raids to break up and deport the migrants, an operational tactic
consistently observed from 2021 through more recent mobilizations in 2025 and
2026. Direct testimonies gathered by academics and independent journalists in
the region reveal institutional tactics of systematic attrition that include
everything from military blockades and physical assaults to the sophisticated
infiltration of undercover agents, who seek to fracture the internal
organization and sow deep discord.

![The Future of Migrant Caravans: Collective Resistance or the End of a
Containment Strategy?](https://mexicosolidarity.com/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/ltam-nov26-07-body-p32.jpg)Illustration: _Let 's Talk
About Migration_, November 2026

The most serious consequence of this institutional harassment is the practical
elimination of collective protection. Abruptly dispersed in the middle of the
road, families are left without communication and far more exposed to the
local and transnational predators they were trying to avoid. Intense fear of
the authorities themselves, who are frequently accused of having high levels
of criminal collusion, drives people to flee along desolate and inhospitable
routes. Emergency health organizations like Doctors Without Borders (MSF)
tirelessly reiterate that blocking mass migration never eliminates the human
desire to migrate; on the contrary, it only increases clinical risk, chronic
physical suffering, and total vulnerability to human trafficking networks at
the regional level.

Given this suffocating context of institutional repression, the future of the
caravans is at a turning point. While the format has not disappeared
entirely—as illustrated by some recent mobilizations in southern Mexico
seeking to appeal to high-level political junctures and changes—its structural
and organizational viability has profoundly mutated due to exhaustion and
fear. Demographic experts and civil society organizations unequivocally agree
that institutional violence is drastically reshaping the dynamics of
migration.

As Mexican security forces refine their protocols for rounding up and
dismantling large groups in the first few kilometers of their journey, the
caravan loses its greatest tactical and historical advantage: the
invulnerability afforded by its size. Consequently, a forced return to
invisibility is now evident. Perceiving that walking in a massive group of
people guarantees confrontations and deportations, thousands are once again
resorting to transnational trafficking networks and the practice of human
smuggling.

The migrant caravans, therefore, are ceasing to be that invulnerable shield of
collective protection and are instead becoming a sporadic expression of
courageous political resistance in the face of humanitarian collapse. New
government restrictions, coupled with severe immigration controls and mass
deportations, have forced the vast majority of the population in transit back
into complete secrecy, dismantling the networks of mutual support that in
previous years saved countless lives throughout the treacherous Mexican
territory.

This punitive dynamic indirectly strengthens the illicit enrichment of
trafficking networks and definitively confirms that forced displacement will
not be halted by mere military presence. The near future of collective
migrations suggests that caravans will continue to exist solely as
intermittent symptoms of systemic crises that erupt when social pressure and
hunger outweigh any well-founded fear of punishment, kidnapping, or official
repression. However, as a sustained survival strategy, this model has been
systematically undermined by the state. The future that awaits thousands of
Central American, South American, and Caribbean families along the route is,
unfortunately, an incessant journey that cruelly mutates, stripping them of
essential collective solidarity and becoming, in an accelerated and tragic
manner, a much more silent, invisible, and lethal passage.
